title: VLANs and Layer 2 on Junos: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Imagine an apartment building with hundreds of residents. There's one mail room with numbered mailboxes. The postie sorts by the number on the envelope, not the contents.

lines.t: Sorted by the number on the envelope

scenes.heading: The mail room
scenes.narration: Each mailbox number is a VLAN. The postie never opens letters, they just read the number. A VLAN is one broadcast domain at layer two. An access port serves one VLAN. A trunk port carries many. Between VLANs, you need a layer three interface.

scenes.heading: VLAN vs subnet
scenes.narration: These two are related, but not the same thing. A V L A N is layer two. A subnet is layer three. You connect them by giving the I R B interface an address. A VLAN lives at layer two, and a subnet at layer three. The address goes on the I R B. Routing needs that layer three interface.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three misunderstandings. A V L A N is not a subnet. Trunks can also connect servers, routers and access points. And a switch won't route between V L A Ns without one.

items.right: VLAN is layer 2; subnet is layer 3
They can connect servers, routers, APs

items.wrong: A switch routes between VLANs on its own

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.cta: Try the Courseiva Junos VLANs lab
scenes.narration: So, to recap. Access ports serve one VLAN, and trunks carry many. The native VLAN is untagged, and both ends must match. Routing between VLANs needs a layer three interface. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva Junos VLANs lab.

points.t: Native VLAN must match at both ends
